subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: Show that the curves y² = 4(x + 1) and y² = 36(9 − x) intersect orthogonally.

mark_split.label: Find both slopes at those points
Show the product of the slopes is −1

recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — say how you find where the two curves meet, and say what orthogonally means in terms of the slopes.

steps.label: Find the points of intersection
steps.margin_note: Two marks, and the two that are most often lost. Both curves give y² in terms of x, so equating the two right sides removes y in one line. Orthogonality is a statement about a COMMON point, so the point must come first.
lines: Given curves:  y² = 4(x + 1)   …(i)   and   y² = 36(9 − x)   …(ii)
At a common point both right sides are equal:
∴ the curves meet at P(8, 6) and Q(8, −6).

recall.must_convey: That equating 4(x + 1) and 36(9 − x) gives x = 8, and then y = ±6, so the curves meet at (8, 6) and (8, −6).
accept: equate the two expressions for y squared and solve for x

steps.why: Two curves are orthogonal at a point they share, so no slope means anything until the shared point is known. Both equations are already solved for y², which is why eliminating y is the shorter route.
common_mistakes: Guessing or assuming a point of intersection instead of solving for it.
Taking only y = 6 and never checking the second point y = −6.
Sign error in 4x + 4 = 324 − 36x, giving 32x = 320 and x = 10.
steps.memory_tip: Both equations start with y², so set the two right sides equal — y disappears without any squaring or substitution.

steps.label: Find both slopes at those points
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Differentiate each curve implicitly and keep the slope in terms of y, because the common points differ only in y. Note the sign: the second curve has −x inside the bracket.

recall.must_convey: That m₁ = 2/y and m₂ = −18/y, so at (8, 6) the slopes are 1/3 and −3.

steps.why: Differentiating 36(9 − x) gives −36, not 36. That single minus sign is what makes the product of the slopes negative, so losing it turns an orthogonal pair into a non-orthogonal one.
common_mistakes: Differentiating 36(9 − x) as +36 and losing the minus sign.
Cancelling 2y into 4 as y/2 rather than 2/y.
Substituting x = 8 into a slope that contains only y.
steps.memory_tip: Both curves are y² = something, so both differentiate to 2y·dy/dx = that something's derivative — only the right side changes.

steps.label: Show the product of the slopes is −1
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Orthogonal means the tangents are perpendicular, that is m₁m₂ = −1. Show it at both common points so the proof covers the whole intersection.
lines: Two curves cut orthogonally at a common point when m₁m₂ = −1 there.

lines.text: ∴ m₁m₂ = −1 at every common point, so the curves y² = 4(x + 1) and y² = 36(9 − x) intersect orthogonally.

recall.must_convey: That orthogonal means m₁m₂ = −1, and the product is −1 at both common points.

steps.why: Orthogonal is a condition on the tangents at the shared point, not on the curves as a whole. Writing the general product −36/y² and then using y² = 36 shows the result holds at both points in one line.
common_mistakes: Checking m₁m₂ = −1 at only one of the two common points.
Using tanθ = |(m₁ − m₂)/(1 + m₁m₂)|, which has 1 + m₁m₂ = 0 in the denominator here and is undefined.
Writing the condition as m₁m₂ = 1 or m₁ = −m₂.
steps.memory_tip: Perpendicular slopes multiply to −1, exactly as in straight lines — at the shared point each curve has the direction of its own tangent.
